newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai merger incentives to rescue sick finance firms.
newsitem.headline: Thai merger incentives to rescue sick finance firms.

text.p: Thailand's moves to shore up its ailing financial sector by offering generous incentives for corporate mergers will help some battered companies from going bankrupt, analysts said on Thursday.
They welcomed fresh incentives set by the Bank of Thailand on Wednesday to encourage 15 commercial banks and more than 90 finance and securities firms to consolidate through mergers.
"It is a very good step in the right direction. This is a pre-emptive measure instead of waiting for a crisis to develop," said Mike Stead, head of research at Union Securities Co.
Central bank governor Rerngchai Marakanond said on Wednesday that financial institutions agreeing to merge could seek licences to undertake a wider range of business.
He said two new commercial bank licences would be made available for newly merged finance institutions with strong capital backing.
He said to promote mergers, Thailand would also relax its 25 percent foreign ownership limit for financial institutions.

"We don't set any foreign ownership limit. Foreign partners can hold over 50 percent, but they will be licensed on a case-by-case basis provided that their presence does not seriously erode competitiveness of Thai companies," Rerngchai told Reuters.
The governor warned that weak, mostly family-run finance companies resisting the policy to merge could rule out chances of getting future financial assistance from the authorities.
"We are using the carrot-and-stick approach. Those not responding will soon get the stick," he told reporters.

The central bank's action follows months of market concern and turmoil over the prospect that finance companies exposed to the troubled property sector could be forced out of business because of liquidity problems.

About a quarter of the loans extended by Thai finance firms went to the property sector, which is struggling through a four-year slump. Foreign analysts estimated that at least 12 percent of the sector's outstanding loans were non-performing.
The central bank in early March ordered 10 cash-strapped finance companies to raise capital to reassure their creditors that the firms could continue to operate soundly.
It also told all financial institutions to increase provisions for sub-standard assets.
Songglod Bhichaikul of United Securities Plc expected at least 20 finance companies to disappear after the first expected wave of officially endorsed mergers in the next one to two years.
"I think the number would be trimmed to about 60. This would be a major restructuring for the industry," he said.
The central bank said bigger finance firms would be permitted after mergers to provide foreign exchange and trade financing services as well as to mobilise retail deposits by issuing bank pass-books.
It said those upgrading into banks, or existing medium and small banks merging with finance firms, could open more branches in crowded urban areas, a practice not promoted by the authorities now.
"The incentives would force small finance firms to merge. The days for family-run finance firms are numbered. Their operating costs would be too high to compete," Songglod said.

"The BOT obviously has more leverage now that finance firms are in trouble," said Stead of Union Securities, referring to Rerngchai's policy to consolidate the sector as it moved to compete in an increasingly liberalised environment.

Stead said of the opportunity for foreign banks seeking to do business in Thailand: "This is the best time for foreign investors to acquire companies here at a cheap price. They could negotiate from a position of strength."
